statement: Ana colours 30 squares in a row: red, red, blue, repeating. Under them, Bo colours 30 squares: red, blue, blue, blue, repeating. How many times is a red square directly above a red square?

choices.misconception: I found 2 matches in every 12 squares and 2 full blocks of 12, but forgot the last 6 squares.
I found 2 matches in every 12 squares, then took 30 divided by 12 as 2 and a half and doubled it.
I counted every place where Bo has red, forgetting that Ana must also have red there.
I counted Ana's red squares and ignored Bo's row.

hints: Bo's red squares are rare, so list their positions. For each one, check what colour Ana has in that place using her cycle of 3.
Bo has red at squares 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29. Ana has blue at every multiple of 3.

solutions.reliable: Bo has red at squares 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29. Ana has blue at 3, 6, 9, ... so at those places she has red except at 9 and 21 (multiples of 3). That leaves 1, 5, 13, 17, 25, 29: 6 places. The transferable idea: with two cycles, list the rarer event and test each one against the other cycle.
solutions.elegant: Both patterns repeat every 12 squares, with red over red at squares 1 and 5 of each block. Squares 1 to 24 hold 2 blocks (4 matches), and squares 25 to 30 match the start of a block, adding 25 and 29: 6 in all.

whyOnTest: Two repeating cycles running together: the combined pattern repeats with the lowest common multiple of the two lengths.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
